Proof: p_{q−1} is the smallest prime ≡ 1 (mod q−1), which is q itself (any prime ≡ 1 mod q−1 is ≥ q, and q qualifies). For m_n: any m < q has φ(m) ≤ m − 1 < q − 1, so (q−1) ∤ φ(m) (φ(m) is positive), forcing m_{q−1} ≥ q; and φ(q) = q−1 shows m_{q−1} ≤ q. Hence m_{q−1} = q = p_{q−1}.

Verified at small parameters: n = 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 22, 28 (n+1 prime) all give equality, e.g. m_4 = p_4 = 5, m_6 = p_6 = 7, m_28 = p_28 = 29.

**The exact reformulation (both directions).**

Call T a φ-witness tree for n: nodes are prime powers; a node r^a is either a leaf or has exactly one child chosen from {r^{a+1}} ∪ {least prime ≡ 1 (mod r^a)}. Define cost(T) = ∏ over distinct root-to-leaf prime labels of the leaf prime (leaves at r^{a+1} count prime r with multiplicity a+1... precisely: cost = ∏_{leaves} ℓ where a leaf at r^{a+1} contributes r, a leaf at a prime ℓ≡1 mod r^a contributes ℓ; multiply over the disjoint prime labels the tree allocates).

- (≤ direction) If T is a φ-witness tree for n with cost c, then n | φ(c): each allocated prime ℓ ≡ 1 (mod r^a) contributes r^a | φ(ℓ) = ℓ−1, and a node terminated at r^{a+1} contributes r^a | φ(r^{a+1}); contributions are on distinct prime factors of c, and φ is multiplicative, so n | φ(c). Hence m_n ≤ cost(T) for every T, so m_n ≤ min_T cost(T).
- (≥ direction) Conversely, given the factorization of any m with n | φ(m), partition the prime-power factors r^a ∥ n among prime factors of m according to which prime q^b ∥ m supplies r^a | φ(q^b) (possible since n | ∏ φ(q^b) and the r^a are coprime, one per distinct r); for each supplied pair, either r^{a+1} | q (then terminate the node at r^{a+1}) or r^a | q−1 (then attach the child q ≡ 1 mod r^a). This extracts a φ-witness tree for n with cost dividing m, so min_T cost(T) ≤ m. Taking m = m_n: **m_n = min over φ-witness trees of cost(T), exactly.**

Note the leaves at ℓ ≡ 1 mod r^a automatically have ℓ ≥ ℓ_{r^a} (R013's demanded ℓ_q repair is built in), and the r^{a+1} branch is why pure "least prime in AP" lemmas were false (their counterexamples at n=3, 9, 16 are exactly instances where the r^{a+1} branch or a shared factor wins).
